passage: The results for the regional science prize went up on the noticeboard at the school in Nairobi, and Vera's name was at the top. She was still smiling when Wanjiru said, not unkindly, "Congrats. Must be easier with a tutor and your own laptop, though." Vera's smile snapped off. "I worked for months! I stayed up every night!" "I know," Wanjiru said. "So did I. On the library computer, when it was free." Vera stomped off, furious. That evening, at her desk under the good lamp, she opened her laptop and stared at it. She had worked hard; every night was true. And Wanjiru had worked hard too, with less. Both things sat there together, uncomfortable. She typed, "Sorry I snapped. Want to use my laptop for the next round?", deleted it, then typed it again.

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru work on the project?
qa.a: On the library computer, when it was free.

qa.q: Why did Vera's smile snap off at Wanjiru's remark?
qa.a: She felt her months of hard work were being dismissed, so she felt attacked and defended herself.

qa.q: What would sending the retyped message show about how Vera's thinking changed?
qa.a: It would show she accepts both truths, her hard work and her extra help, and wants to share the advantage rather than deny it.

qa.q: What was it like for Wanjiru to hear "I stayed up every night!"?
qa.a: Wanjiru may have felt unheard, having worked hard too but with far fewer tools, which was the whole point.

grounding: A teenager told she had it easier snaps back that she worked hard, then realises her effort and her advantage are both real.

passage: In the corridor of the coaching centre, the new batch list was taped to the glass. Tanuja had made the top batch. Zeenat, who hadn't, looked at the list for a long time. "Of course. Your dad pays for the extra test series, and you've got a room of your own to study in." Tanuja's ears went hot. "Excuse me? I did four hours every day. I gave up dance for this." "I'm not saying you didn't work." "Then what are you saying?" "That I did four hours too, in a kitchen with my brothers." The bell rang and they walked in apart. All through physics, Tanuja kept hearing it. The test series did help. The quiet room did help. That didn't make her four hours fake. It just meant Zeenat's four hours had cost more.

qa.q: What did Tanuja give up for her studies?
qa.a: She gave up dance.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling and realising all through physics?
qa.a: She felt defensive yet uneasy, realising that the test series and quiet room helped her without cancelling her own four hours a day.

qa.q: What could Tanuja say to Zeenat after class that holds both truths?
qa.a: She could say, "You're right, I had help you didn't, and I also worked hard," and perhaps offer to share the test papers.

qa.q: What was Zeenat trying to get Tanuja to see?
qa.a: Zeenat wasn't denying Tanuja's effort, only pointing out that the same four hours cost more in a crowded kitchen.

grounding: A teenager told she had it easier responds that she worked hard, then sees that effort and unearned advantage can both be true.

passage:
Kavitha,
I've started this letter three times. The first two were angry.
When you said at the bus stop that I only made the state swimming team because Appa pays for the club pool and the coach, I wanted to shout. I've been in that pool at 5 am since I was nine. My shoulders ache every winter. I felt like you'd rubbed all that out in one sentence.
But then I remembered you practising in the river near your grandmother's village in the holidays, because there's no pool near you, and still reaching district level.
So here's what I think now. I did work hard. And I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me at 5 am. Both are true. One doesn't erase the other, but I shouldn't pretend the second isn't there.
Can we talk tomorrow?
Shalini

qa.q: At what time has Shalini been in the pool since age nine?
qa.a: At 5 am.

qa.q: Why did Shalini's first two letters come out angry?
qa.a: Kavitha's remark made Shalini feel that years of 5 am practice had been rubbed out in one sentence.

qa.q: What changed Shalini's mind, and what did Shalini choose to do?
qa.a: Remembering Kavitha practising in the river helped Shalini see both truths, and Shalini chose to admit the advantage and ask to talk.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading "I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me"?
qa.a: Kavitha would likely feel heard, since the point was never that Shalini was lazy, only that the start was different.

grounding: A teenager who felt attacked on being told they had it easier writes back acknowledging both years of hard work and real unearned advantages.

passage: So, Chacha, you asked about the state orchestra. I'm Divyansh, first violin, yes, thank you. But the day the list came out, Tamanna, who plays viola, said, "Of course you got in. You've had a private teacher since you were five. I learnt from videos on a borrowed viola." I got so angry. I said, "I practised two hours every single day! Nobody handed me anything!" and walked off. I was fuming the whole way home. That night I sat with the violin case open and thought about it properly. The two hours were real. My blisters were real. But so was the teacher, and the good violin, and Mamma driving me to every lesson. Tamanna practised too, just without any of that. Both things are true, and the second one doesn't erase the first. I haven't said this to Tamanna yet. I'm working out how.

qa.q: How did Tamanna learn to play?
qa.a: From videos, on a borrowed viola.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh get so angry at Tamanna's words?
qa.a: Divyansh felt the two hours of daily practice were being brushed aside, as if the place had simply been handed over, so the comment felt like an attack.

qa.q: What turning point came that night, and where could it lead?
qa.a: Sitting with the violin case, Divyansh saw that the practice and the head start were both real; the next step is telling Tamanna so, without taking back the effort.

qa.q: How might Tamanna have felt when the list went up?
qa.a: Tamanna had practised on a borrowed viola with no teacher, so the list may have felt like proof the race was uneven, whatever effort Divyansh put in.

grounding: A teenager told they had it easier snaps back about daily practice, then sees that the hard work and the head start are both true.

passage: I'm Harpreet, and I was holding the water bottles when it happened. Devika had just won the inter-school tennis final. She was glowing. Nilesh, who'd lost in the semis, shook her hand and said, "Well played. Bit easier with a club court and a coach, though." He said it quietly, not nastily. Devika's face changed. "Excuse me? I'm up at five every day. I've cried on that court. You think it's easy?" She grabbed her bag and walked off. Nilesh just stood there. He practises on the cracked concrete court behind the municipal school, with a racket he taped up himself. On the bus back, Devika was quiet, staring out. Near her stop she said, not to anyone exactly, "The five a.m. is real. The coach is real too, I suppose." I don't know if she'll say it to Nilesh. I hope so.

qa.q: Where does Nilesh practise?
qa.a: On the cracked concrete court behind the municipal school.

qa.q: What does Devika's quiet line on the bus suggest she was beginning to feel and think?
qa.a: It suggests her anger was cooling into an uneasy honesty: her early mornings were real, and so was the advantage of a coach and a club court.

qa.q: What choice does Devika face after the bus ride, and what might she say?
qa.a: She can stay defensive or go back to Nilesh; she might say, "I did work hard, and you're right that I had help you didn't."

qa.q: How might the final have looked to Nilesh, with his taped-up racket?
qa.a: Nilesh wasn't denying her effort, only naming the uneven start, and her anger may have left him feeling he wasn't allowed to say it 😔

grounding: A teenager who wins is told it came easier with a coach, reacts as if attacked, and later begins to see that hard work and advantage can both be true.
